slides.title: Chapter 13: Bitcoin Security
slides.sub: What a signature protects, how keys are kept and backed up, and how several keys survive loss and theft. Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are Recorded.
slides.notes: This deck explains Bitcoin security: what a signature protects, how traffic and the chain's first block are trusted, how a download is checked, and how keys are kept offline, on a device, behind a passphrase and in a backup. It ends with several keys, a delayed heir and Shamir's shared secrets. Every example runs under Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run on a test network, so its answers are Recorded and only read back here. The research package for chapter 13 holds the sources and the claims.

slides.title: Trusting the network and the software
slides.sub: What a signature protects, and what a node or a download is trusted for.
slides.notes: This part asks what Bitcoin protects and what it asks you to trust. A signed payment cannot be altered or replayed, node traffic is now encrypted by default, the chain starts from one typed-in block and a shortcut called assumed-valid, and a downloaded program can be checked against a list of hashes, but only so far as the signers' keys are known.

slides.title: A signature protects value and recipient
slides.sub: Like a cheque with amount and payee inked in: change either and the signature fails

rows: s, t, r = R['b1_secrecy'], R['b1_tamper'], R['b1_replay']
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest

items: Row 2: the 222-byte payment holds a 71-byte signature and the 33-byte public key, no private key and no WIF
Row 3: a valid payment is accepted; a swapped recipient or a changed amount breaks the signature
Rows 4 and 5: the sighash byte 01 signs all outputs; a replay pays nothing, the outputs are already known

items.body: NOT EXECUTED: real money on mainnet; every payment here was made on regtest.

slides.notes: A Bitcoin payment authorizes a specific value to a specific recipient. On a Bitcoin Core 31.1 test node, a signed payment of 222 bytes held a signature of 71 bytes and the public key of 33 bytes, and neither the private key nor its WIF text. The same payment with a swapped recipient or a changed amount was refused, because the signature covers the outputs, and sending it again paid nothing. No mainnet funds were used.
slides.take: A signature covers value and recipient, and never contains the key

slides.sub: Like sealing the envelope: strangers on the road cannot read it, only the two peers can

slides.notes: The book says that no encryption is required for Bitcoin traffic, and chapter 10 says Bitcoin Core talks in the clear. That is out of date: BIP 324 defines an encrypted version 2 transport, release 26.0 added it switched off, and release 27.0 turned it on by default. Two test nodes of Core 31.1 spoke v2 and agreed on one session id, while a peer without v2 was still served over v1. No traffic was captured on the wire.
slides.take: Since release 27.0 peers encrypt their traffic by default

slides.title: The root of trust: one typed-in block
slides.sub: Like tracing a family tree to its founder, but trusting a recent page to save time

items.label: executed on blocks saved from mempool.space and on the saved chainparams.cpp

items: Row 2: the hash of the first block is typed into chainparams.cpp, and the code asserts it (True)
Rows 3 and 4: Core 31.1 also ships an assumed-valid block, 938,343, and may skip script checks for blocks before it
Row 5: that block is 33,237 blocks behind the tip, so 'trust only a validated chain' has a shortcut

slides.notes: The book says that the genesis block is the root of trust and that the only thing to be explicitly trusted is a fully validated blockchain. The genesis hash is indeed typed into chainparams.cpp and asserted. But Bitcoin Core 31.1 also ships an assumed-valid block, 938,343, and its help says a node may assume that block and its ancestors are valid and skip their script verification. Trust is therefore in the release you installed as well.
slides.take: The chain starts from one typed-in block, plus an assumed-valid shortcut

slides.title: Does the download match the list?
slides.sub: Like a seal on a medicine box: it shows the box is the listed one, not who sealed it

items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the list and the Guix text are saved

items: Row 2: the SHA-256 of the 90,293,352-byte tarball equals its line among the 28 in SHA256SUMS (True)
Row 3: gpg checked none of the 11 signatures with an empty keyring: exit 2, no good signature
So the hash shows the file is the listed one, not who listed it; Guix builds avoid blind trust (row 4)

items.body: NOT EXECUTED: a good gpg verification; it needs the builders' public keys, which were not imported.

slides.notes: The tarball of Bitcoin Core 31.1 has 90,293,352 bytes and its SHA-256 equals its line in the list of 28 hashes, so it is the file that the list names. But the list itself is signed with 11 signatures, and with an empty keyring gpg could call none of them good: the hash proves only that the file is the listed one. The project's Guix builds exist so that users need not trust binary downloads blindly.
slides.take: A matching hash proves the file is the listed one, not who listed it

slides.title: Keeping the keys safe
slides.sub: Cold storage, devices, passphrases, backups and seed words.
slides.notes: This part is about keeping keys. A watch-only wallet and a partially signed transaction keep the keys on another machine, a hardware wallet makes the signature and defends itself with waiting, a passphrase locks the wallet file, and a backup must hold the descriptor and be recent. Seed words are checksummed arithmetic. The stories are the Trezor and the Casascius coin.

slides.title: Cold storage: watch, sign elsewhere, send
slides.sub: Like a cashier who writes cheques and a manager in another building who only signs them

rows: h, c, b = R['b3_hot'], R['b3_cold'], R['b3_broadcast']
"Can't get private descriptor string for watch-only wallets"
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest, three nodes

items: Row 2: the hot wallet has private keys disabled and cannot sign (complete False, no signatures)
Row 3: asked for its private descriptors, a watch-only wallet refuses: it holds none
Rows 4 and 5: a node with 0 blocks and 0 connections signed the 528-character PSBT; the hot node sent it

items.body: NOT EXECUTED: a true air gap; the cold node was a second regtest node, not a separate machine.

slides.notes: In cold storage the node that is online holds only public keys. On test nodes the hot wallet had private keys disabled and could not sign, and when asked for its private descriptors it answered with error minus four. A second node with no blocks and no connections signed the partially signed transaction of 528 characters, and the hot node finalized and broadcast it. A second node on the same machine is not a true air gap.
slides.take: The online wallet only watches; the signing happens somewhere else

slides.title: Hardware wallets wait and wipe
slides.sub: Like a safe that makes you wait longer after each wrong code, and then empties itself

items: Row 2: waits 1, 2, 4 ... 16,384 s add up to 32,767 s, 9.1 hours
Row 4: four words fall in 17.6 s at a trillion guesses a second
Row 5: after 16 failed PIN entries the device wipes itself (True)
Row 6: -signer drives a device. NOT EXECUTED: a device

items.title: Seconds of waiting after the nth wrong PIN

rows: tries = 15; wait = [2 ** k for k in range(tries)]
seen('bitcoinwiki_trezor.txt', 'wipe itself after 16 failed PIN entry attempts')
items.label: executed on the Bitcoin Wiki and the Core documentation, saved on 2026-10-15

slides.notes: A hardware wallet holds the keys and defends them with a PIN whose waits double after every wrong try: they add up to 32,767 seconds, 9.1 hours, before the device wipes itself at the sixteenth. A phrase a person invents is weaker: four words from a list of 2,048 give 17,592,186,044,416 phrases, which an assumed trillion guesses a second exhaust in 17.6 seconds. Bitcoin Core can drive such a device with the option -signer, and the person must still read the address on the device's screen; no device was run.
slides.take: The device protects the key; you must still read the address on its screen

slides.title: A passphrase locks the keys, not the balance
slides.sub: Like a locked cash drawer in a shop window: customers see the money, only you can open it

rows: l, w, u, f = R['b4_locked'], R['b4_wrong'], R['b4_unlocked'], R['b4_file']
('wallet encrypted; The keypool has been flushed and a new HD ', False)
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the constants are read from the saved crypter.h

items: Row 2: a locked wallet shows its balance (1.0) but cannot send (-13); a wrong passphrase gives -14
Row 3: an unlock for 3 seconds ended exactly then: the key is dropped and sending fails again
Rows 4, 5: 32-byte key, 8-byte salt, 25000 rounds; encrypting also makes a new seed, so old backups miss new coins
Row 7: 25,000 rounds take 0.1 s on a 1.86 GHz Pentium M: 1,242.8 days to try every 30-bit passphrase

slides.notes: Encrypting the wallet locks the private keys and nothing else. A locked test wallet still showed its balance but refused to send with error minus 13, a wrong passphrase gave minus 14, and a three-second unlock ended on time. The key is AES-256 with 8 bytes of salt and 25000 rounds, about 0.1 seconds on an old laptop, so trying all 30-bit passphrases takes about 1,242.8 days on one such machine. Encryption also makes a new seed, so an older backup misses new coins.
slides.take: Encryption hides the keys, and it starts a new seed: back up again

slides.title: A backup is a descriptor and a date
slides.sub: Like a spare key cut before the locksmith adds new locks: it opens only the old ones

rows: (sum(c for i, c in paid if i < pool), sum(c for i, c in paid))
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the pool count is worked by hand

items: Row 2: a wallet restored from a fresh backup holds all 3.0 coins and derives the same next addresses
Rows 3, 6: with a keypool of 3 a stale backup held 1.0 of 3.0: coins at address 9 lie outside 0 to 2 (1 of 3 by hand)
Row 4: one key does not know the multisig address; the descriptor finds the 2.0 coins, a wrong key order 0.0

items.body: NOT EXECUTED: paper and metal backups; only file backups of regtest wallets were restored.

slides.notes: The book speaks of a wallet as keys that can be backed up like any file. In Bitcoin Core 31.1 a wallet is a set of descriptors, and a backup is only good while it is recent: with a keypool of 3 a stale backup held only 1.0 of 3.0 coins, because 2.0 went to the tenth address, and counted by hand 1 of 3 comes back. For a multisignature wallet the descriptor must be saved too, since one key alone knew nothing of the address.
slides.take: A backup needs the descriptor and a recent date

slides.title: Seed words and their arithmetic
slides.sub: Like a recipe card: twelve words are enough to cook the same keys again

rows: ent = 16; cs = ent // 4; words = 12; total = words * 11; tcs = total - total * 32 // 33
items.label: executed on the published BIP 39 test vector, saved on 2026-10-15; the Core files are saved

items: Rows 2, 4, 5: 16 bytes make 12 words with a 4-bit checksum; a random wrong phrase still passes 1 time in 16
Row 6: 2048 rounds with the passphrase TREZOR give the published seed (True); with none the seed starts 5eb00bbd
Row 7: no mention of a mnemonic in Core's descriptors document or help: Core keeps descriptors, not words
NOT EXECUTED: recovery of a BIP 39 phrase in Bitcoin Core; Core has no such import.

slides.notes: A seed phrase is a number written in words with a checksum. Sixteen bytes of entropy, 128 bits, get a 4-bit checksum and make twelve words from a list of 2048, so a random wrong phrase still passes once in 16. The seed is made with 2048 rounds of PBKDF2 over the words and an optional passphrase, and it equals the published Trezor vector. Printing a single key on paper was a method of 2011 to 2016 that the Bitcoin Wiki now calls obsolete.
slides.take: Twelve words with a checksum rebuild every key; Core itself keeps descriptors

slides.notes: A Trezor holds the keys and makes the signatures, and it defends itself against a thief with a PIN whose waits double, with a wipe after 16 failed attempts. SatoshiLabs announced the Trezor Safe 5 on 14 June 2024 at BTC Prague, with a colour touchscreen and an EAL 6+ secure element. The Bitcoin Wiki still warns that malware could swap the recipient's address, so the person must read the address on the device's own screen.

slides.notes: Mike Caldwell of Sandy, Utah, made physical bitcoins: a coin with a private key under a tamper-evident hologram, sold in sizes from 1 to 1000 BTC. FinCEN had told him that minting physical bitcoins qualified him as a money transmitter that must register, and he suspended sales on 26 November 2013. The book's physical storage, the seed on paper or metal, is the same idea without the maker.

slides.title: Surviving loss and theft
slides.sub: Several keys, a delayed heir and shared secrets, and what custody costs.
slides.notes: This part is about the two ways to lose coins, losing the key and having it stolen. Several keys, a path for an heir that opens after a wait, and Shamir's shared secrets each trade one risk for another, and the odds depend on what is feared. The stories are the exchange that held everyone's keys and the paper that began secret sharing.

slides.title: Two of three keys sign
slides.sub: Like a safe deposit box that needs two of three keyholders: one lost key is no disaster

items: Row 2: one signature is incomplete, two complete: 146 virtual bytes
Row 3: lose one key: spendable (True); lose two: not (False)
Row 4: one key 110 virtual bytes, 2-of-3 146; sortedmulti True
Row 6: by hand: 146 virtual bytes, 1,460 satoshis at 10 each

rows: s, l, o = R['b6_sign'], R['b6_loss'], R['b6_order']
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest

slides.notes: A two-of-three wallet needs two signatures: on the test chain one signature left the payment incomplete and two made it complete, in 146 virtual bytes against 110 for a single key. Counting the bytes by hand gives the same 146, which is 1,460 satoshis at 10 per virtual byte. The loss of one key left the funds spendable, the loss of two did not. With sortedmulti the address is the same for any order of the keys, which is why the descriptor belongs in the backup.
slides.take: Two of three keys survive one loss, and cost 36 more virtual bytes

slides.title: Odds of losing or being robbed
slides.sub: Like extra locks on a door: fewer break-ins, but more ways to lock yourself out

items: Row 1: lost at 0.1: 2-of-3 stuck 0.028, 1-of-3 0.001
Row 2: stolen at 0.05: 2-of-3 robbed 0.00725, 1-of-3 0.14263
Rows 3, 4: the binomial terms summed by hand give the same 0.028
Rows 5, 6: and the same 0.00725; the keys are assumed independent

rows: from math import comb; n = 3; m = 2; p = 10; q = p / 100
round(sum(comb(n, s) * (1 - q) ** s * q ** (n - s) for s in range(m)), 4)
round(sum(comb(n, s) * q ** s * (1 - q) ** (n - s) for s in range(m, n + 1)), 5)
items.label: executed on the chapter's own formulas; the chances are assumptions

slides.notes: The odds depend on what is feared. If each key is lost with chance 0.1 and stolen with chance 0.05, independently, which is an assumption, a two-of-three setup is stuck with chance 0.028 and robbed with chance 0.00725, against 0.1 and 0.05 for one key. A one-of-three setup is almost never stuck, 0.001, but is robbed with chance 0.14263. Summing the binomial terms by hand gives the same 0.028 and 0.00725.
slides.take: More keys trade the risk of loss against the risk of theft

slides.title: An heir who must wait ten blocks
slides.sub: Like a will with a waiting period: the heir can claim only after the owner stays silent

items: Rows 2, 3: the owner spends at once; the heir is refused at 1 and 9 confirmations and accepted at 10
Rows 4, 6: older(65536) was accepted by Core 31.1, but 65536 & 65535 is 0: the heir could spend after 1 block
Rows 6, 7: the longest honest wait is 65,535 blocks, 455.1 days; ten blocks are 100 minutes, ten 512-second units 85
NOT EXECUTED: estate planning with a lawyer; only the script rule was tested, on regtest.

slides.notes: A wallet can give an heir a path that opens only after a delay: the policy was or(owner, and(heir, older 10)). On the test chain the owner could spend at once and the heir was refused at one and nine confirmations and accepted at ten, about 100 minutes of blocks. The trap: BIP 68 keeps 16 bits, so older(65536), which Core 31.1 accepted, means a wait of 0 and the heir could spend after one block. The longest honest wait is 65,535 blocks, about 455 days.
slides.take: An heir path waits for confirmations, and a value over 65,535 wraps around

slides.title: Shamir: three pieces, any two open it
slides.sub: Like a map torn in three: any two pieces show the spot, one shows nothing

rows: p = 11; y = 5; fits = {(s, (y - s) % p) for s in range(p)}
(len(fits), len({s for s, a in fits}), p)
items.label: executed on the chapter's own Shamir library over a prime field

items: Rows 2, 3: a secret is split in three shares; any two recover it, one share alone does not (False)
Rows 4, 5: modulo 11, one share fits all 11 possible secrets, one slope for each: the secret stays undetermined
The chapter does not mention Shamir; BIP 93 (codex32, a draft) and SLIP 39 use the idea for seed words

items.body: NOT EXECUTED: Shamir sharing inside a wallet; the shares were made by the chapter's own library.

slides.notes: Shamir's scheme splits a secret into n pieces so that any k of them recover it and fewer reveal nothing. In the chapter's library a secret was split into three shares, and any two returned it while one share did not. Over the small prime 11, one share fitted 11 pairs of secret and slope, one for each of the 11 possible secrets, which is what undetermined means. The book does not mention the scheme, but BIP 93, a draft, and SLIP 39 use it for seed words.
slides.take: Any two of three shares recover the secret, and one share reveals nothing

slides.title: The exchange that held the keys of everyone
slides.sub: The story of 24 February 2014: who, where, when and what to read next

items: Mt. Gox, Shibuya, Tokyo, suspended all trading on 24 February 2014
850,000 lost bitcoins, 7 percent of all coins: about 12.1 million (row 1)
Bitfinex, 2016: a 36 percent cut, so 40 kept 25.6 (row 2)
850,000 less 199,999.99 found: 650,000.01 (row 3). NOT EXECUTED: a breach

items.who: Mark Karpeles, who bought the site in March 2011 and ran it as CEO, Jed McCaleb, who founded it
items.where: the exchange Mt. Gox in Shibuya, Tokyo, Japan, and its website mtgox.com

slides.notes: Mt. Gox of Shibuya, Tokyo, launched in 2010, halted withdrawals on 7 February 2014 and suspended all trading on 24 February. The 850,000 bitcoins it reported lost were called about 7 percent of all coins, which implies a supply near 12.1 million. Counts differ by source: 850,000 less the 199,999.99 found leaves 650,000.01. Bitfinex in 2016 cut every account by 36 percent, so 40 bitcoin kept 25.6, and customers of both held claims, not keys.

slides.title: Three pieces of a key, any two will do
slides.sub: The story of 1 November 1979: who, where, when and what to read next

items.cap: Adi Shamir Royal Society - Duncan Hull, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: In November 1979 Adi Shamir, then at MIT, publishes How to Share a Secret in the Communications of the ACM
Modulo 47, the secret 12 and slope 30 give shares 42, 25 and 8; two of them give back 12 (row 2)
With 3 of 5 shares needed, 16 groups open the secret and the 10 groups of two learn nothing (row 4)

rows: from math import comb; n = 5; k = 3
(sum(comb(n, j) for j in range(k, n + 1)), comb(n, k - 1))
items.label: executed on small numbers worked by hand, after the published 1979 paper

items.who: Adi Shamir, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and co-inventor of RSA, and the editor Rivest of the Communications of the ACM
items.where: the Communications of the ACM, volume 22, number 11, November 1979, pages 612 and 613
items.linkText: Shamir: How to Share a Secret (PDF, 1979)

slides.notes: Adi Shamir's paper How to Share a Secret (Communications of the ACM, November 1979) divides data into n pieces so that any k compute it and any k minus 1 leave it completely undetermined. It rests on polynomial interpolation: k points fix one polynomial of degree k minus 1, and the secret is its value at zero. Modulo 47, the secret 12 and slope 30 give shares 42, 25 and 8, and two of them return 12. With 3 of 5 shares needed, 16 groups open the secret and 10 groups of two learn nothing.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per idea, each one provable from its slides

Keys are safer offline or on a device, behind a passphrase, and backed up with their descriptor

Several keys, a delayed heir or shared secrets trade the risk of loss against the risk of theft
